To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) The students who were interviewed were not particularly concerned about NAPLAN, but they were concerned about being judged as a ‘bad’ maths student; (2) Students who were interviewed were concerned about being labelled as ‘bad at maths’ and being judged by their parents and teachers; and (3) The students were concerned about being compared to other students and being labelled as ‘good’ or ‘bad’ at maths.
In summary, our research is concerned with
exploring the attitudes towards NAPLAn numeracy tests of students, parents and teachers in two schools.
exploring student, parent, and teacher attitudes towards the NAPLAN tests.
exploring how students, parents and teachers understand the NAPLAN numerary tests and the impact they have on students’ learning of mathematics.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the NAPLAN numerate testing is an effective tool for identifying students who require additional assistance with numerate skills.
the NAPLAN tests are not a reliable indicator of a student’s mathematics ability.
NAPLAN testing in years 3 & 5 is a waste of time for all stakeholders involved and that it does not improve the learning of mathematics.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
NAPLAN numeracay tests are not a useful tool for measuring student achievement in mathematics.
the results of this research indicate that there are no winners from high stakes testing.
there are no clear winners from high stakes mathematics testing.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the NAPLAN tests are not helping to improve mathematics education in Australia.
NAPLAN tests do not provide any useful information to students, parents or teachers.
the high stakes NAPLAN tests are not working for the students, parents, teachers and schools involved.
